Article Title: Retired wind turbines are being transformed into tiny solar-powered houses and recycled skis by a Swedish company
Article Text:
Image credit: Vattenfall

From blades to buildings

Recycling wind turbine blades is still a challenge

As much as wind turbines are important, once their blades are decommissioned, all that's left for them is to live in landfills for years. Europe is on track for a record win year, with 8.8 GW of new capacity installed in the first half of 2026, a 30% jump year on year. That’s enough electricity to power around seven million European households and replace fossil fuel imports equivalent to 25 LNG tankers a year, according to industry nonprofit WindEurope.But for every turbine that goes up, one comes down. And manufacturers are still trying to figure out how to make sure that none of the materials goes to waste. While 90% of a wind turbine's mass is made of easily recyclable materials like steel, copper, aluminium and concrete, composite materials make up the majority of their blades, and this is where the problem arises. “Separating the composite materials from the resin requires specialised processes, often involving high temperatures or other energy-intensive treatment methods,” Eva Julius-Philipp, Director of Environment and Sustainability of Business Area Wind at Vattenfall, told Euronews Earth. “In some cases, these processes can affect the quality and value of the recovered materials, making large-scale recycling more challenging.”Since the landfill ban on blades, nacelle covers and nose cones in 2021, the Swedish startup Vattenfall has come up with some creative alternatives, with houses and skis being some of them.From the ground or even further away, the grandeur of wind turbines often goes unnoticed. Putting it into perspective, Vattenfall teamed up with design studio Superuse to turn a retired wind turbine nacelle cover – which houses the mechanical and electrical equipment – into a compact living space. Four metres wide, 10 metres long and three metres high, the box once sat atop an Austrian wind turbine. It’s now a tiny house fitted with a kitchen, bathroom and living space equipped with a heat pump, solar panels and a solar water heater. It was showcased at Dutch Design Week in 2024 as part of an initiative exploring how materials could be reused with as little energy- and emissions-intensive processing as possible.Blades, as well, have been re-envisioned as building materials. After being decommissioned in 2023, the 57 blades from the Danish onshore wind farm Nørre Økse Sø found new life as a facade for a multi-storey car park in the city of Lund. It’s opened the door to a multitude of inventive uses for retired blades, from frames for solar panels to alpine skis.“Projects such as the Tiny House, blade-based building projects and recycled skis are not yet a large-scale solution, however, they are intended to help us gain experience, develop new applications and stimulate the market for circular solutions,” said Julius-Philipp.Provided it’s safe to do so, extending the operational lifetime of existing components through reuse and refurbishment is the preferred option, she added.Wind turbine blades can be between 50 and 100 metres long and are designed to spin in harsh weather for up to 25 years. What makes them so durable is also what makes them difficult to recycle: materials such as glass fibre, carbon fibre, epoxy resin, balsa wood, metals and various fillers pressed tightly together in layers.Aiming to achieve 100 per cent circularity for these composite materials by 2030, Vattenfall is working on new ways of reusing, repurposing, refurbishing and recycling blades. “When composite materials cannot be recycled at a high value, they can be processed through energy recovery and/or cement co-processing,” said Julius-Philipp.Currently, Vattenfall uses mechanical recycling processes to turn blade material into composite flakes or fillers for new products, while pyrolysis, a thermal recycling process, recovers fibres and other secondary materials. As the first generation of major European wind farms reaches the end of its operational lifespan in the coming years, more blades will enter retirement, increasing the need for solutions that are “scalable, cost-efficient and low in energy use,” she added.The EU has not yet enforced a ban on landfilling decommissioned blades. Only Austria, Finland, Germany and the Netherlands have their own binding national bans, and WindEurope is now pushing Brussels to make the commitment legally binding across all member states.“What is needed now is a regulatory framework that enables circular value chains and secondary raw materials to scale,” said Julius-Philipp, who hopes the European Commission’s Circular Economy Act, expected to be proposed later this year, will help provide it.
Article Summary: Recycling wind turbine blades is still a challenge. Europe is on track for a record win year, with 8.8 GW of new capacity installed in the first half of 2026. Vattenfall is working on new ways of reusing, repurposing, refurbishing and recycling blades.

Article Title: In 2024, Narelle Zanker turned her 4,000-acre family dairy farm into a classroom; 2 years later, her Dairy Adventures had welcomed 1,200+ visitors and won the 2026 Rural Women’s Award
Article Text:
Photo: dairyadventures/ Instagram

From classroom to cowshed

A farm that teaches

Recognition and next steps

Why the story matters

In 2024, Narelle Zanker turned her 4,000-acre family dairy farm near Mannum into a living classroom where visitors could bottle-feed calves, watch milking in action and learn where their food really comes from. Two years later, her agritourism venture Dairy Adventures had welcomed more than 1,200 guests and earned her the 2026 AgriFutures Rural Women’s Award for South Australia, followed by the national title at Parliament House in Canberra. According to AgriFutures Australia, the former teacher was recognised for bridging the gap between farmers and consumers through hands-on education and regional tourism, with new plans to reach even more students through virtual farm lessons and school resources.Narelle Zanker grew up on her family’s mixed farming property near Mannum, about an hour east of Adelaide on the Murray River. After spending four years working as a school teacher, she returned to the farm with a clear idea. She wanted to combine her love of education with her lifelong connection to dairying. With support from her husband Joel and wider family, she launched Dairy Adventures in 2024 as the only agritourism experience of its kind in South Australia.The venture operates on a working 4,000-acre dairy and mixed farm that milks around 300 cows with year-round calving. Instead of a static display farm, visitors step into a real food production facility. They tour the dairy, watch mechanised milking in action, learn about calf rearing and biosecurity, and hear how milk moves from paddock to plate. Zanker has woven teaching frameworks into every tour so that preschoolers, school groups, families, aged-care residents and disability groups all leave with a clearer picture of modern farming.Dairy Adventures runs up to four tours a week and offers experiences that feel more like play than a lecture. Guests bottle-feed calves, try their hand at milking, meet the herd and even visit favourites like Elvis the steer. For many city families and grandparents, these moments reconnect them with rural life they remember from their own childhoods. For students, the visit becomes a living science lesson about animal care, food safety and the systems behind everyday groceries.In its first year alone, the business welcomed more than 1,200 visitors and earned a silver medal in the New Tourism Business category at the 2025 South Australian Tourism Awards. That rapid growth showed there was strong demand for transparent, paddock-to-plate experiences that let people ask questions and see the work behind their food.Zanker’s work caught the attention of AgriFutures Australia, which runs the Rural Women’s Award to celebrate innovation and leadership by women in regional industries. In May 2026 she was named the South Australian winner, receiving a $15,000 Westpac grant to improve accessibility on the farm, develop interactive features and create educational resources with Dairy Australia. She also planned a children’s book about life on a dairy farm for schools and libraries.Later that year, she took the next step by winning the national AgriFutures Rural Women’s Award at a gala dinner at Parliament House in Canberra. As national winner she received an additional $20,000 grant to expand Dairy Adventures further, including building a virtual classroom program so students across Australia can join live lessons from the farm even if they cannot visit in person.At a time when fewer Australians live on farms, initiatives like Dairy Adventures help rebuild trust and understanding between producers and consumers. Zanker has said the goal is not just to show a pretty farm, but to help people see the science, systems and care in every bottle of milk. By turning a working dairy into a classroom, she is creating a new model for agricultural education that is both commercially viable and deeply community focused.
Article Summary: Narelle Zanker won the 2026 AgriFutures Rural Women’s Award for South Australia. The former teacher was recognised for bridging the gap between farmers and consumers through hands-on education and regional tourism. She has plans to reach even more students through virtual farm lessons and school resources.

Article Title: A Georgia city moved a pre-Civil War house out of the way of a hotel project instead of demolishing it; after a $500,000 relocation and restoration, it is becoming a coffee shop
Article Text:
The nearly $500,000 relocation and restoration effort has preserved the pre-Civil War structure, which is now being prepared as a new location for Bizarre Coffee (Image Credit: Facebook/ @Save Acworth History by Mark Turner)

A historic house gets a second chance

The move was part of a wider effort to preserve the building's historic character while giving it a practical future (Image Credit: Facebook/ @Save Acworth History by Mark Turner)

Moving the house instead of tearing it down

From family home to coffee shop

A preserved landmark with a new purpose

A house that survived for more than a century is getting a new life not as a museum, but as a place for coffee and community. In Acworth, Georgia, the historic McCray House was moved from its original site to make way for a new hotel, rather than being demolished. The nearly $500,000 relocation and restoration effort has preserved the pre-Civil War structure, which is now being prepared as a new location for Bizarre Coffee. According to Bizarre Coffee's official Acworth page, the company's forthcoming shop will operate inside the historic McCray House at 4415 Cherokee Street, next to Logan Farm Park.The McCray House dates to the mid-1800s and is one of Acworth's surviving historic structures. The house later became closely associated with the McCray family, who acquired it in the 1960s. Over the years, the property became part of the community's social life, with family events, weddings, holiday celebrations and a petting zoo among the memories associated with the home. When redevelopment was planned for the property's original location, the city chose to relocate the structure instead of allowing it to be lost.CBS Atlanta reported in March 2026 that a new hotel was being developed on the original lot and that the city spent $500,000 to move the house and repurpose it as a coffee shop.The City of Acworth purchased the abandoned 19th-century property and approximately three acres in 2021. Earlier plans involved transferring the house to Cobb Landmarks for restoration and use as an event and exhibit space, but the nonprofit eventually stepped away from the proposal because of budget considerations. In 2025, the city's Board of Aldermen approved $84,800 for architectural and engineering services connected with the relocation.Relocating a historic house is far more complicated than simply transporting a building from one address to another. According to CROFT & Associates, which worked with the City of Acworth and Macallan Construction, the McCray Farmhouse was separated from later additions, placed on steel beams and transported along Cherokee Street to its new location at the entrance to Logan Farm Park.The move was part of a wider effort to preserve the building's historic character while giving it a practical future. The City of Acworth's project updates also linked the relocation to plans for a new hotel on the property's original site. Jeff Chase, Acworth's director of downtown development, tourism and historic preservation, told CBS Atlanta how the new foundation was prepared. Chase said the structure was positioned over a cinder-block wall, with the wall then being built upward to meet the bottom of the house.For members of the McCray family, the project also represented the preservation of decades of personal memories. Speaking to CBS Atlanta, Moose McCray recalled the house's connection to weddings, children and community gatherings and said he was glad that the property would be preserved.The next chapter for the building is considerably different from its earlier roles. Bizarre Coffee is preparing to open its Acworth location inside the restored McCray House. The company's official website currently lists the location as "coming soon" at 4415 Cherokee Street and describes it as a historic home that has been part of the Acworth community for generations. Bizarre Coffee also says the future shop will sit beside Logan Farm Park, include an outdoor patio, and retain much of the historic house's character. The company has described the project as the next chapter for the building as it prepares to become its Acworth location.The City of Acworth celebrated the restoration with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on July 16, 2026. The city said the project team had worked to maintain the historic integrity of the building while allowing its story to continue through a new use. The City of Acworth also noted that Sabrina Kaylor, owner of Bizarre Coffee, would bring new memories to the property when the shop opens. The restoration work has included attention to the building's exterior and interior character. Macallan Construction, one of the project's partners, said the work included a new roof, exterior siding, refinished floors and restoration of intricate porch details as the house was prepared for its new use as Bizarre Coffee.The McCray House is therefore becoming an unusual example of adaptive reuse. Instead of remaining an abandoned structure or disappearing beneath redevelopment, the historic house has been physically moved, restored and given a commercial purpose. Its future as a coffee shop also means the building will remain part of everyday life in Acworth. Visitors will be able to use a structure that dates back to the mid-19th century while experiencing a completely different chapter of its history.For a house that has already passed through multiple generations, survived major changes around it and moved to a new location, its next chapter will begin with something much simpler: coffee, conversation and another generation of community memories.
Article Summary: The McCray House in Acworth, Georgia, was moved from its original site to make way for a new hotel, rather than being demolished. The nearly $500,000 relocation and restoration effort has preserved the pre-Civil War structure, which is now being prepared as a new location for Bizarre Coffee. The City of Acworth purchased the abandoned 19th-century property and approximately three acres in 2021.

Article Title: The man considered the world's last royal coachmaker died at 76 before finishing a 3-tonne carriage for King Charles III; his team says it is now 98% complete
Article Text:
Frecklington's fascination with coachmaking began when he was just eight years old.

A final gift to the crown

From a pony cart to royal carriages

A legacy built on wheels

A craft that may never be repeated

For more than half a century, Jim Frecklington turned wood, metal, leather and gold into something increasingly rare: magnificent horse-drawn carriages built by hand. His workshop on Sydney's northern beaches became the unlikely birthplace of vehicles destined for royal ceremonies, but his final project was also his most personal. Frecklington died at 76, leaving behind a three-tonne carriage for King Charles III that is now nearly complete, states an online report by ABC Information and Services. Scroll down to read the details.Frecklington died in an aged care facility in Manly after a lengthy battle with cancer. Despite receiving a terminal diagnosis while the Commonwealth Royal Coach was still under construction, he continued working toward completing the decade-long project, adds the report. The carriage is now about 98 percent finished, according to members of his team, who are completing the final details, the report said. The enormous coach was financed in part by remortgaging Frecklington's home and was designed as a tribute to more than 1,000 years of British monarchy and the Commonwealth.If we go by the online reports, its details reflect the extraordinary level of craftsmanship that went into the project.Hand-applied gold leaf covers much of the coach, while timber from Westminster Abbey forms part of its construction. Despite its traditional appearance, the carriage incorporates modern comforts, including electric windows and air conditioning.Frecklington's fascination with coachmaking began when he was just eight years old. Growing up in Parkes, New South Wales, he struggled to ride his Shetland pony and found another solution which was of building a cart for the animal to pull. That childhood experiment eventually led him around the world. After graduating from The Scots College in Sydney in 1968, Frecklington spent time in the Arctic operating heavy equipment used in the construction of airstrips. He moved to England four years later and worked at Windsor Castle, caring for the Duke of Edinburgh's four-in-hand horses, states ABC report. He later joined the Royal Mews in London, where he worked with Queen Elizabeth II's ceremonial horses.Frecklington's connection to the British royal family continued after he returned to Australia. In 1977, he was invited to manage Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee Exhibition during its Australian tour and created a replica of Edward VII's 1902 State Landau. His work soon reached an even grander scale. He built the Australian State Coach as Australia's Bicentennial gift to Queen Elizabeth II in 1988 and later created the Diamond Jubilee State Coach for her 80th birthday in 2006. According to the report, the Diamond Jubilee coach eventually played a role in King Charles III's coronation because the Commonwealth Royal Coach was not yet ready.Frecklington leaves behind three carriages associated with the British royal family and a reputation built on craftsmanship rather than mass production. His approach was famously hands-on, relying heavily on experience and an ability to visualize complex designs without conventional plans. Now, his final carriage is being completed by the craftsmen who worked alongside him. When finished, the Commonwealth Royal Coach will stand as more than a ceremonial vehicle. It will be the final chapter of a remarkable career and a lasting example of a traditional craft that Frecklington spent his life keeping alive.Images Courtesy: ABC Information and Services
Article Summary: Jim Frecklington died at 76, leaving behind a three-tonne carriage for King Charles III. The Commonwealth Royal Coach is now about 98 percent finished, according to members of his team, who are completing the final details. The enormous coach was designed as a tribute to more than 1,000 years of British monarchy and the Commonwealth.

Article Title: North America loses its monopoly on dinosaur fossils; fourteen tail vertebrae just turned up in Spain and experts have identified it as Diplodocus
Article Text:
Identifying the first Diplodocus fossils

Large pneumatic cavities inside the vertebrae

Deep longitudinal grooves along the underside of the tail bones

Distinctive forked chevron bones with unique medial fossae

Elongated vertebral centra without lateral ridges

From North America to Spain

Palaeontologists in Spain have discovered the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils outside of North America, marking the first-ever discovery outside the area. For 150 years, every confirmed bone of the animal came from one place, the Morrison Formation of western US. But recently, Sergio Sanchez Fenollosa and his colleagues found the same anatomical signature in a set of tail vertebrae found in Teruel, Spain.The roughly 150-million-year-old remains turned out to be the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils ever found outside North America, the team reported in the Journal of Vertebrate Palaeontology. During the Late Jurassic, falling sea levels may have exposed land that dinosaurs could walk across between the continents. “With each new result, the picture became clearer: we were looking at a Diplodocus,” Sánchez Fenollosa, the study’s lead author, said in a press release.The first five vertebrae turned up at La Tejeria back in 2008. It wasn’t until excavations in 2014 and 2015 that the team recovered nine more, along with several chevrons, the bones attached beneath the tail vertebrae. Some of the vertebrae were still connected in the order they’d been in while the animal was alive.The whole find covered roughly 108 square feet (10 square meters).According to Alberto Cobos, one of the study's co-authors, the animal was about 82 feet long. But even that partial tail is among Europe’s most complete finds from the dinosaur’s wider family. Earlier finds from this family in the region included a tooth and scraps of hip and tail bone.Sánchez Fenollosa, Cobos, and co-author Josué García Cobeña measured the bones by hand with callipers or a tape measure and compared them with published descriptions of other long-necked, plant-eating sauropods. The vertebrae had deep grooves running underneath and no ridges along the sides, while the chevrons were forked.The excellent preservation of the specimen allowed the researchers to recognise several anatomical traits associated with Diplodocus, including:The team recognised that combination in Diplodocus and checked the identification with computer analyses of the animals’ relationships. The results shuffled other parts of the family tree around, but every version placed the Spanish dinosaur on the Diplodocus branch.Diplodocus now joins Allosaurus and Stegosaurus among dinosaurs from the Jurassic rocks on both sides of the Atlantic. It ranks among the most recognisable dinosaurs ever discovered. It is known for its enormous length (up to 25 meters), long whip-like tail, and relatively small head.Since Diplodocus was first discovered in the United States in 1878, casts of its skeleton have appeared in major natural history museums around the world, particularly during the early 20th century. Those displays helped turn Diplodocus into an international symbol of palaeontology and one of the most familiar dinosaurs in popular culture.At the time these animals lived, the ocean was still opening between the continents. As sea levels fell, stretches of land may have appeared between what’s now Newfoundland and the Iberian Peninsula, home to modern Spain and Portugal. Those temporary routes could have offered animals a way to wander from one continent to the other. However, it still remains unknown to the researchers exactly when Diplodocus crossed between them or which route it took.The team can identify the animal as Diplodocus, but the tail doesn’t preserve enough detail to pin down its species. In their analyses, the Spanish animal came out closest to the North American species Diplodocus hallorum. Finding a more complete skeleton in Europe could help them work out just how closely the two were related.The sediments surrounding the bones were deposited on a coastal plain shaped by rivers. Other enormous plant eaters, including Turiasaurus and Losillasaurus, also lived in what is now Teruel, Cobos notes in the Dinópolis Foundation’s press release. These dinosaurs belonged to a different branch of the sauropod family.The original tail bones are now on display at Dinópolis in Teruel, while visitors in El Castellar can see replicas of the bones unearthed nearby.
Article Summary: For 150 years, every confirmed bone of the animal came from the Morrison Formation of western U.S. But recently, Sergio Sanchez Fenollosa and his colleagues found the same anatomical signature in a set of tail vertebrae found in Teruel, Spain. The roughly 150-million-year-old remains turned out to be the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils ever found outside North America.

Article Title: In 2014, Leonardo DiCaprio's foundation donated $1 million, helping save African elephants who were being killed for their ivory tusks at a rate of 100 per day
Article Text: Illegal hunting and the ivory trade have reduced the populations of elephants in Africa drastically over the past century. Millions of these mammals once roamed the iconic jungles, but their long ivory tusks made them targets of big game hunters and poachers who have decimated their numbers by roughly 95% over the past 100 years. The ivory trade drives a brutal campaign of international poaching that killed 22,000 elephants in 2012 alone, despite a global ban on the sale of ivory.According to the World Wildlife Fund for Nature (WWF), there are an estimated 415,000 African elephants, but other organisations put their numbers even lower, claiming that those "may ultimately prove to be optimistic."In order to save the elephants, a joint initiative was launched by Save the Elephants and the Wildlife Conservation Network, titled the Elephant Crisis Fund. Started in 2013, it had an initial target of raising $5 million over three years to provide funding for global projects to stop poaching, trafficking and the demand for ivory.In 2014, at a gala in Malibu held in support of the fund, they made major progress toward the goal. Hollywood legend Leonardo DiCaprio ended up giving the initiative not only his star power, but also a $1 million grant from his foundation, the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation.“Elephant poaching is a brutal crisis, with more than 30,000 elephants killed last year alone. The decimation of these animals is something we have the power to stop, and the Elephant Crisis Fund is a crucial part of the solution,” said the Hollywood actor in a statement. In total, the Elephant Crisis Fund raised $2 million during the 2014 Malibu gala.Douglas-Hamilton, a researcher who has spent more than 50 years studying elephants in the wild, is the founder of Save the Elephants. “The only future for elephants is for governments, organisations, and individuals to join together in their support,” said Douglas-Hamilton back in 2014. “What we have seen in Los Angeles has given us greater hope than ever, as a generous donation by the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation was matched by this astonishing community. ”The event was attended by a number of Hollywood stars including director Rupert Wyatt, singer Barbra Streisand, actor Jonah Hill, Glee star Dianna Agron, actor Dermot Mulroney, Snow White And The Huntsman actress Liberty Ross, Interscope Records co-founder Jimmy Iovine, and Mad Men actress Elisabeth Moss.Then in 2016, Netflix released a documentary, 'The Ivory Game', produced by DiCaprio, that Indiewire described as 'a real-life ecological thriller' about the illegal ivory trade. “If James Bond turned his attention to animal rights issues, he might find himself in the middle of this hidden war,” the publication said.That same year, the United States took action to stop illegal poaching and protect endangered elephants by imposing a near-total ban on the commercial trade of African elephant ivory in order to reduce global demand. Many countries followed suit, including Hong Kong, which was the primary transit and processing hub, and China, which overtook Japan as the world’s largest importer of ivory in the 2000s.Over the past ten years, the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), says that elephant poaching and ivory trafficking have gone down overall. However, other groups still state numbers in excess of 30,000 as there is no hard reliable data. “The only future for elephants is for governments, organisations, and individuals to join together in their support,” said Iain Douglas-Hamilton, founder of Save The Elephants.Over the years, DiCaprio has been heavily invested in animal conservation. In 2013, he hosted an art auction raising $38.8M for global conservation initiatives. His foundation has given $3 million for Oceana’s ocean conservation programs and $3 million for WWF’s tiger program in Nepal.Recently, he and the Bezos Earth Fund launched the Phoenix Species Project, an initiative dedicated to recovering endangered species. The $200M fund will provide support to recover 100 species facing imminent extinction spanning mammals, amphibians, reptiles, birds, fish, invertebrates and plants from 30 countries in habitats ranging from oceans to volcanic plains.

Article Title: US extends visa curbs on Palestine officials, blocks President Abbas from UN General Assembly
Article Text:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas appears on a screen as he addresses the 80th United Nations General Assembly (UNGA)

The United States has extended visa restrictions on Palestinian Authority officials and members of the Palestine Liberation Organization, preventing President Mahmoud Abbas and other Palestinian officials from travelling to the US ahead of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.According to Reuters, the US state department said it had determined that the Palestinian Authority and PLO continued to engage in actions that Washington considers inconsistent with commitments made under US laws. The restrictions come ahead of the annual UN gathering, where Palestinian statehood and the Israel-Palestinian conflict are expected to remain major issues.The state department said the Palestinian leadership had continued to pursue measures against Israel through international bodies, including the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Washington also cited efforts to secure international recognition of a Palestinian state outside negotiations with Israel.The US has previously said such actions violate commitments made by the Palestinian Authority and PLO under the PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 and the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002. The administration also cited what it described as payments to individuals involved in terrorism and the glorification of terrorism.The restrictions are tied to two US laws governing Palestinian commitments. The PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 requires Washington to assess whether the PLO is meeting commitments on recognising Israel, accepting UN resolutions and renouncing violence.The Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002 similarly requires the US to assess compliance by the PLO and Palestinian Authority with commitments made during the Oslo peace process, including resolving outstanding issues through negotiations and peaceful means.The restrictions will prevent Abbas and other affected Palestinian officials from travelling to New York for the UN General Assembly. The US imposed similar visa restrictions last year, and the latest decision extends those measures ahead of this year’s UN session.The state department said the restrictions do not apply to Palestinian officials covered by a waiver for the Palestinian Mission to the UN. The waiver allows accredited Palestinian diplomats to enter the US and participate in UN-related activities despite the broader visa restrictions.The US decision comes as the Palestinian leadership faces growing diplomatic pressure over its international campaign for recognition of statehood and legal action against Israel. Washington has repeatedly opposed efforts to pursue Palestinian statehood through international forums rather than through direct negotiations with Israel.
Article Summary: US state department said it had determined that the Palestinian Authority and PLO continued to engage in actions that Washington considers inconsistent with commitments made under US laws. The restrictions come ahead of the annual UN gathering, where Palestinian statehood and the Israel-Palestinian conflict are expected to remain major issues.

Article Title: Australia to bar foreign students from bringing families, target 225,000 net migration by 2028
Article Text:
Australia home affairs minister Tony Burke is expected to announce the changes.

New restrictions on student families

Migration becomes a political issue

Student numbers and pressure on housing

Australia is preparing to stop international students from bringing their partners and children with them while they study, as the government moves to reduce migration and tighten rules for temporary visa holders, media reports said on Thursday.Home affairs minister Tony Burke is expected to announce the changes in a speech at the National Press Club later in the day. The government plans to bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 by 2028, compared with about 300,000 currently, public broadcaster ABC News reported. Burke's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Under the current system, international students can bring dependent children under 18 to Australia. Their spouses or partners are also allowed to work, although the number of hours they can work depends on the student's course.The proposed changes would remove the option for students to bring their families while they study. The government is also expected to tighten rules governing temporary migrants who want to switch to another visa.The announcement comes as the hard-right One Nation party gains support in recent polls and pushes for a much larger reduction in temporary migration.The party said this week that it wanted to cut the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over three years, giving Australians "breathing space".One Nation describes its approach as "Australia first" and has proposed reducing net overseas migration to 130,000 after the initial three-year period. It says the programme would be reviewed every year.Australia's migration intake rose sharply after the country reopened its borders in February 2022, following nearly two years of Covid restrictions. International students, backpackers and temporary skilled workers contributed to the increase.Migration has since declined over the past two years, but critics continue to argue that high numbers of newcomers are putting pressure on housing and infrastructure and affecting social cohesion.Official figures show net overseas migration reached 306,000 in the year to June 30, 2025. International students accounted for more than half of that total. Net migration stood at 429,000 in 2024, after reaching a record 518,000 in 2023.The proposed restrictions would affect international students and other temporary migrants, as the government seeks to reduce the overall number of people entering and remaining in Australia.
Article Summary: Government plans to bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 by 2028. Under current system, international students can bring dependent children under 18 to Australia. Their spouses or partners are also allowed to work, although the number of hours they can work depends on the student's course.

Article Title: US likely committed war crimes in Iran strikes that killed over 150: UN
Article Text:
On February 28, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, southern Iran, killing at least 156 people, including about 120 children

School strike killed 120 children

Iran crackdown also amounted to crimes against humanity

UN human rights experts have found “reasonable grounds” to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran that killed over 150 civilians, including around 120 children. The findings were published by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran in a report to the UN Human Rights Council.The mission examined two of the deadliest attacks on civilians after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28. It concluded that a missile strike on a primary school in Minab and another attack on a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd amounted to indiscriminate attacks that caused civilian deaths and damaged civilian objects.The findings come as the UN faces wider concerns over violations of international law in conflicts involving powerful states. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has warned that the growing geopolitical divide and paralysis at the Security Council have created an environment of impunity, with powerful countries flouting international law and the UN Charter.On February 28, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, southern Iran, killing at least 156 people, including about 120 children, according to local authorities.The fact-finding mission said the school was clearly identifiable and found no information indicating that it was being used for military purposes.The school was next to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex that was also attacked that day. However, the experts concluded that the school was the intended point of impact and that the damage was not the result of an errant missile or collateral damage. Survivors told investigators that the school was struck twice.The experts cited media reports that a preliminary US military inquiry had found US forces responsible, along with the fact that the US was the only party in the conflict known to possess Tomahawk missiles. On that basis, they said there were "reasonable grounds to believe" the US carried out the strike.The US military has not released the findings of its investigation. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".In Lamerd, Precision Strike Missiles dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and nearby residential area, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities. The mission again found the site clearly identifiable and no indication that it was being used for military purposes.The experts cited the US possession of PrSM missiles as part of the evidence linking the attack to Washington. The US military, however, has denied carrying out strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon as a PrSM.The report also documented widespread violations during Iran's crackdown on mass protests in December 2025 and January 2026. The mission said killings by security forces occurred on "a staggering and unprecedented scale" across all 31 provinces.At least 221 children, some as young as two, were reportedly killed. Security forces also attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded protesters and detaining healthcare workers, which the experts said discouraged victims from seeking life-saving treatment.Tens of thousands of people were arbitrarily detained and faced "torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal advice". At least 29 men were executed following expedited trials linked to the protests, while more than 70 people, including five women and three boys, remained at imminent risk of execution.The mission said "many of these grave violations amount to crimes against humanity – including murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians."The experts called on Iran and the US to immediately cease violations and crimes, compensate victims and ensure such acts are not repeated. They also urged independent investigations into alleged violations by all parties and accountability for those responsible.
Article Summary: UN human rights experts have found “reasonable grounds” to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran. The strikes killed over 150 civilians, including around 120 children. The findings were published by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran in a report to the UN Human Rights Council.

Article Title: 'A bit chubby': Memoir claims King Charles fat-shamed Diana; was 'giddily elated' by her death
Article Text:
File photo: Princess Diana and then-Prince Charles at their wedding

‘Like a lottery winner’ after Diana’s death

Charles fat-shames Diana

‘We’ll forget her soon enough’

Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, is set to release a memoir that makes a series of deeply personal claims about his sister’s relationship with King Charles, alleging that the then-Prince Charles sounded “giddily elated — like a lottery winner” when he called after Diana’s death in 1997 and that he once told her, shortly after their engagement, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”The allegations appear in Spencer’s forthcoming memoir titled ‘Swan Song: Diana, My Sister’, which is being serialised ahead of its publication. The book draws on Spencer’s recollections of his sister’s life, marriage and death nearly three decades ago.Buckingham Palace has already issued an unusually strong response to the book’s claims. While saying it does not comment on books as a matter of principle, a Palace spokesperson said King Charles was mindful that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory” even many years after a loss.Spencer writes that he was at his home in Cape Town with his children when he learnt that Diana had been killed in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997.After a series of calls confirming her death, Charles called Spencer, according to the memoir.Spencer claims that while other callers were stunned and struggled to express their condolences, Charles “sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner”.He says Charles told him he had informed William and Harry of their mother’s death in their bedrooms at Balmoral.Spencer describes the conversation as “strangely matter-of-fact” given the circumstances.Looking back, Spencer says he suspects Charles may have been thinking about how Diana’s death could free him to marry the woman he loved, an interpretation that forms part of Spencer’s own recollection of the conversation.Another claim concerns Diana’s weight and eating disorder in the months before her wedding.Spencer writes that Diana was already struggling with an eating disorder when Charles allegedly squeezed her waist shortly after their engagement and remarked: “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”He says the comment devastated Diana. According to Spencer, she later told him that her waist shrank from 29 inches to 23½ inches between her engagement and wedding.Spencer also claims that Diana had told a friend that Charles had confided to her on the eve of their wedding that he was happy to marry her but was not actually in love with her.Spencer recounts another alleged conversation with Charles during preparations for Diana’s funeral.He says he objected to William and Harry walking behind their mother’s coffin and subsequently received a call from Charles. Spencer describes Charles as becoming angry during the exchange.He claims that Charles eventually told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough!”Spencer writes that he was so shocked by the remark that he told Charles he could not believe he had said it before ending the call.The Palace’s response came after this earlier extract was published. It did not directly address the individual allegations but questioned the reliability of memories shaped by grief decades after Diana’s death.The memoir also contains claims about Diana’s funeral arrangements, her decision to divorce Charles, her relationship with the royal household and her experiences during the breakdown of her marriage. Spencer says the book is intended, in part, to challenge what he considers “untruths” that emerged after his sister’s death.
Article Summary: Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, is set to release a memoir that makes a series of deeply personal claims about his sister’s relationship with King Charles. Spencer alleges that the then-Prince Charles sounded “giddily elated — like a lottery winner” when he called after Diana’S death in 1997. He also claims that he once told her, shortly after their engagement, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?”

Article Title: US grants visas to Iran's Pezeshkian, Araghchi for UNGA amid war with Tehran
Article Text:
The move comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran

Iran delegation to face restrictions

US warns against ‘shopping sprees’

The US has approved visas for Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other members of Tehran’s core delegation to attend next week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York, despite the two countries remaining locked in a war that is entering its seventh month.The State Department said the decision was consistent with Washington’s obligations as the host country of the UN, but stressed that the Iranian delegation would face restrictions during its stay. The delegation will be subject to limits on movement and barred from purchasing luxury and certain other goods.The move comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran, with the conflict having disrupted energy markets and expanded beyond Iran’s borders since it began in February.“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level week,” the State Department said.It added that the delegation would be placed under travel restrictions and face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods under existing US policy. The department also said Iran’s delegation would be smaller than last year’s.The US has previously imposed restrictions on Iranian officials attending the UN. Last year, Iranian diplomats were barred from shopping at wholesale clubs such as Costco and required permission to purchase luxury items including jewellery, alcohol and cars.State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott criticised Iranian officials over their planned visit, accusing them of seeking to use the UN General Assembly for luxury shopping while ordinary Iranians face economic hardships.“While ordinary Iranians endure brutal repression, water and electricity shortages, and soaring inflation, the regime's officials want to go on shopping sprees in New York. Not on our watch,” Pigott said in a post on X.He added that the US would continue to prohibit Iranian UN Mission officials, visiting officials and their dependents from buying wholesale club memberships or luxury goods.
Article Summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other members of Tehran’s core delegation will attend the UN General Assembly in New York. The State Department said the decision was consistent with Washington's obligations as the host country of the UN. The delegation will be subject to limits on movement and barred from purchasing luxury and certain other goods.

Article Title: In 2025, Florida salvagers found more than 1,000 gold and silver coins from a 1715 wreck off the Treasure Coast; the salvage company estimated the haul at $1 million
Article Text:
Representative image of salvagers recovering gold and silver coins from a centuries-old shipwreck beneath the ocean. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

The hurricane that changed Florida's coast

A cache hidden beneath the sand

Representative image of an underwater archaeological team excavating a centuries-old shipwreck artefact from the seabed. Image Credit: ChatGPT.

What happens to the recovered coins?

For more than three centuries, the Atlantic waters off Florida have held reminders of a Spanish fleet that met disaster on its journey home. In 2025, divers returned to that underwater landscape and recovered a remarkable cache of more than 1,000 gold and silver coins. The discovery, made during the summer salvage season, was estimated by the salvage company at about $1 million, adding another chapter to one of Florida's most famous shipwreck stories.According to the Associated Press, the artefacts include 1,051 silver reales, five gold escudos, and other gold objects recovered along Florida’s Atlantic coast. The coins have been identified as having been struck in the Spanish colonies of Mexico, Bolivia, and Peru. Many of the coins still bear dates and mint marks. Captain Levin Shavers and his crew aboard the M/V Just Right carried out the recovery for 1715 Fleet – Queen’s Jewels LLC. They are responsible for the exclusive salvage of the wrecks.The coins had lain on the seabed for nearly 310 years since the hurricane struck the Spanish treasure ships, which were travelling from Havana to Spain on July 31, 1715. The ships carried gold and other valuables the Spanish had collected from their colonies in the Americas. According to NOAA , about 2,500 sailors and passengers were aboard the fleet, and around 1,000 died when the hurricane struck.The disaster scattered wreckage and treasure along Florida’s east coast, with the surviving material eventually contributing to the area’s association with treasure hunting and the name “Treasure Coast”.The hunt for that lost treasure is nothing new. Salvage activities have been taking place for decades, with treasure hunters recovering coins and other items from these shipwrecks. Kip Wagner is among those who made their mark as an early salvor, with thousands of silver coins being retrieved by his crew in the 1960s.The discovery made in 2025 seems to have been very localised in its nature. Many of the coins were found in one place, and the salvagers think they may originally have been stored in a bag or bundle that broke apart when the ship sank. Some of the coins reportedly had marks suggesting they had been inside a burlap bag. The dates found on the coins also give us some idea of the money that may have been carried aboard the ship shortly before its sinking. Reports about the discovery say some of the coins date from the late 17th century to 1714, reflecting the range of currency that could have been in circulation when the 1715 fleet set sail.According to the National Park Service , shipwreck sites can provide valuable archaeological evidence about maritime trade and past societies, making the location and relationship of artefacts important beyond their monetary value. A coin recovered from its original archaeological setting can provide information about its date, mint and movement, while its position alongside other objects can help researchers reconstruct patterns of trade and exchange across the Spanish Empire. It is especially significant in Florida, where the practice of treasure recovery is long intertwined with archaeology. Underwater cultural resources in Florida are regulated, and removing historic artefacts from state-owned waters without proper authorisation is illegal. The 1715 Fleet–Queens Jewels project carries out its operations through authorised salvage agreements.However, the salvaged fragments do not just end up being taken out of the ocean and exhibited. The artefacts get catalogued first, and information like the age, mint markings, weight and recovery location of each coin is recorded. Afterwards, the coins undergo conservation, which includes cleaning aimed at removing the salt deposits while preserving the metal structure.Under Florida's system, the state may keep some of the recovered archaeology for study and exhibition. The rest is split up in accordance with the salvage contracts and judicial supervision involved. This suggests that more artefacts may still be buried under the sand. More than 300 years after the fleet sank, changing sea floors, weather, and shifting sands continue to uncover artefacts that were hidden for centuries. For treasure hunters, the discovery is a major find. But for historians and archaeologists, the importance of the find is that the 1,000-plus coins might be able to tell them much about the people who went on the journey in 1715.
Article Summary: Divers recovered 1,051 silver reales, five gold escudos, and other gold objects along Florida’s Atlantic coast. Coins have been identified as having been struck in the Spanish colonies of Mexico, Bolivia, and Peru. Many of the coins still bear dates and mint marks.

Article Title: Trump extends $100K H-1B visa fee until Sept 2027 but court stay remains: White House cites plunge in filings by IT cos
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump

Read also:

and

Core takeaways:

The Extension: The White House has extended the Sept 19, 2025 proclamation imposing a $100K fee on certain H-1B petitions through Sept 21, 2027.

The Legal Status: Because the original 2025 framework was vacated by a federal district court, the extended fee policy inherits the same legal block, meaning USCIS remains barred from collecting the $100K fee for now. As was reported by TOI the US federal appeals court refused to stay a lower (district) court’s order that had struck down the controversial $100k fee on H-1B visa applications for new workers hired from outside the US. The plaintiffs in this case were 20 US states.

The Compounding Threat: In addition to the proclamation fee, USCIS has separately proposed a regulation that would impose a fee of more than $103K on all cap-subject H-1B petitions—creating a potential multi-layered financial hurdle for employers.

Read also:

Key statistics and claims from the White House proclamation:

Over 700 petitions paid: The administration reports that the $100K fee payment has been submitted for more than 700 petitions (H-1B visa applications) since its implementation in Sept 2025.

92% plunge in H-1B registrations by large IT outsourcing firms: The White House credits the restrictions with a massive reduction in registrations from large IT staffing and outsourcing firms dropping from 24,946 down to just 2,055 filings, a 92% decrease.

Consular requests collapse: Consular processing requests aimed at bringing overseas workers directly into the US fell by nearly 97% between the FY 2025 and FY 2027 cap seasons.

Surge in beneficiaries holding a Master's degree: There has been a shift in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with registrations for beneficiaries with at least a US. Master’s degree rising from 45.1% of total registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1% for FY 2027. Further job offers with wages corresponding to the two highest wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3% of H-1B registration selections while those corresponding with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8%.

The Indian workforce connection:

Initial employment dominance: According to official USCIS data for the fiscal year ended Sept 30, 2025, India-born beneficiaries accounted for 50.3% (57,747 out of 114,806) of H-1B petitions approved for initial employment.

Continuing employment strength: The concentration was drastically higher among renewals: India-born beneficiaries accounted for a massive 77.6% (226,359 out of 291,542) of H-1B petitions approved for continuing employment, anchoring senior engineering and tech operations across corporate America.

In a major development especially for Indian tech professionals who constitute a fair chunk of H-1B visa holders and American sponsoring companies, US President Donald Trump has issued a fresh presidential proclamation extending the controversial $100K H-1B visa fee for another 12 months, stretching the policy through Sept 21, 2027.However, immigration attorneys emphasize that despite the White House's aggressive push, the fee remains legally blocked by a federal court order.Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm explained, “The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) remains barred from collecting the $100K H-1B fee under the Sept 2025 proclamation, which was due to expire on Sept 21, 2026. Since the new proclamation is issued as an extension, USCIS should be barred from collecting the $100K fee under the new proclamation as well. If USCIS takes the position that the new proclamation is outside of the purview of the existing court order, plaintiffs in the ongoing litigation are likely to quickly challenge that view. ”Greg Siskind, co-founder at Siskind Susser, an immigration law firm pointed out that the language is virtually identical in the new proclamation, but the new version states that the fee applies to people seeking admission from outside the US (via consulates or ports of entry)—turning previous agency guidance into official proclamation text.The preamble to this proclamation explicitly states that: “Finally, my Administration continues to explore other complementary efforts that would, among other things, reform the H-1B program and assist with cost-recovery for immigration program administration.”Siskind adds that this signals that the Trump administration may try to implement permanent high fees through the standard rule making process of notice-and-comment.Furthermore, sponsoring employers could also face a compounding financial squeeze from a separate proposed regulation targeting an additional $103K fee, which would not only apply to H-1Bs who were outside US and were selected in the lottery, but will also cover students from within the US who are transiting from a F-1 visa to an H-1B.Wexler adds, “In addition, last month, USCIS separately proposed a regulation that would impose a fee of more than $103K on all cap-subjectH-1B petitions. That fee would be separate from and in addition to the $100K H-1B proclamation fee, where applicable, if the proclamation fee were to be reinstated by further court order.”Thus, if the proclamation fee is ultimately revived by higher courtsthe separate USCIS cap-subject fee rule goes into final effect, affected employers could theoretically face cumulative financial barriers totaling over $200K per petition (application) for sponsoring H-1B cap workers.The newly released White House proclamation details several official metrics highlighting the administration's policy impacts since the original Sept 2025 order:Indian nationals especially those in the tech sector represent the absolute backbone of the H-1B programme, making any major shifts in policy disproportionately impactful on the Indian diaspora, even as reliance on H-1B visas by Indian tech companies has significantly reduced.According to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP) only three Indian-based companies in FY 2025 were among the top 25 employers with approved H-1B petitions for initial employment. In FY 2025, the top seven Indian-based companies had only 4,573 H-1B petitions approved for initial employment, a 70% drop from FY 2015 and 37% fewer than in FY 2024.However, Indians continue to dominate the H-1B visa holders spectrum.With the White House doubling down on its high-skilled immigration overhaul even as federal courts block its path, stakeholders on both sides of the Atlantic are bracing for a prolonged legal showdown. For India’s massive tech diaspora and the corporate giants relying on their expertise, the coming months will test the limits of executive power over America's borders.
Article Summary: The White House has extended the Sept 19, 2025 proclamation imposing a $100K fee on certain H-1B petitions through Sept 21, 2027. Because the original 2025 framework was vacated by a federal district court, the extended fee policy inherits the same legal block, meaning USCIS remains barred from collecting the fee for now.

Article Title: From 2020 to 2023, Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste for cultch and reef-replenishment work along its Gulf Coast
Article Text:
AI Representation: Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste. Image credits: Chatgpt

How the funding and structure came together

Why shell cultch matters more than most substitutes

Sunlight eliminates all bacteria and organic materials in the shells. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

"Restoration Is a Partial But Not Complete Solution for Long-Term Declines in Oyster Populations: A Case History From the Northeastern Gulf of America,"

What sets Mississippi's approach apart

From 2020 through 2023, the state of Mississippi ran a shell collection and recycling pilot program that redirected discarded shells from Gulf Coast restaurants and put them back into the water as cultch, which is the hard material that young oysters use to cling to in order to grow. The pilot program was conducted under the initiative “Save Our Shells,” and helped solve an issue which had gone unnoticed in the Gulf region: as the industry shifted away from centralized shucking toward selling live oysters directly to restaurants, the resulting shells became scattered across many small locations rather than concentrated at a few processing plants, leaving them a largely uncollected resource.According to MDEQ and RESTORE Council program documentation, the Mississippi Sound Oyster Shell Recycling Program was funded with a RESTORE Act grant of approximately $650,000, drawn from civil penalty funds tied to the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and designated for Gulf Coast restoration and recovery. The funds were used for Mississippi's Oyster Shell Recycling Pilot Project to recycle oyster shells from restaurants.The department contracted The Nature Conservancy to manage the program, with the first phase spent on planning before the shell collection itself launched in 2023. After the construction process, the restaurants retain the shucked shells for reuse, where contractors come by to transport the shells to a location for exposure to sunlight for many months, thus eliminating all bacteria and organic materials in the shells before placing them in the ocean. Cultch production is then transferred to the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to use in the replenishment of the oyster reefs in coastal areas within the state.Oysters require something hard to settle on, but shell is often preferred by oysters as cultch over concrete, limestone, and gravel. An article in the Marine Ecology Progress Series researched Louisiana’s Sister Lake and found that oyster biomass from reefs made using shell cultch reached 14.6 kilograms per square meter after three years, with faster shell accretion than reef subsidence. The same Marine Ecology Progress Series also noted that the reef growth trajectory was unique to each site: reefs situated less than 8 kilometres apart grew in different ways, with recruitment and mortality differing greatly across sites. Nonetheless, within just three years, all the reefs harbored high numbers of oysters averaging 728 ± 102 per square meter, and the growth of the shell exceeded the local needs to match the rates of subsidence and shell erosion.Suwannee Sound provides a parallel view from a different perspective. Oyster density was monitored over fourteen years, nine years before and five years after a massive restoration of limestone beds. The number of oysters per square meter at the newly restored sites rose from nearly zero to 91 in six months and to 244 in five years. The study,led by W.E. Pine and USGS colleagues and published in Marine and Coastal Fisheries: Dynamics, Management and Ecosystem Science , found that rebuilding hard substrate was an essential step in reef recovery, though the paper's title itself signals that restoration is only a partial, not complete, solution to long-term oyster decline.The project carried out in Mississippi has been somewhat different since it used a single grant that has covered its funding throughout several years instead of starting the project step-by-step in restaurants. Such an approach has allowed setting a rather high collection goal; however, it implied spending the first few years not on getting results but on planning and building the collection infrastructure. The project itself is quite consistent with the findings of the research, since the shells, which might otherwise be sent to a landfill, is now used to recreate reefs that will contribute to the process of filtering the water as well as the development of recreational and commercial fisheries.
Article Summary: Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste. Sunlight eliminates all bacteria and organic materials in the shells. Cultch production is then transferred to the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to use in the replenishment of the oyster reefs in coastal areas.

Article Title: In 2020, BSEE reported 43 retired Gulf platforms had joined Rigs-to-Reefs since 2017, providing habitat where more than 100 fish species live
Article Text:
Gulf of Mexico. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

California research measured record fish production on platform structures

Louisiana survey found the same pattern at a converted platform reef

A Rice whale in the western Gulf of Mexico. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Reefing costs less than full platform removal

Hundreds of aging oil and gas rigs in the Gulf of Mexico are decommissioned each year. While federal regulations demand that these rigs be dismantled once they are no longer operational, more and more rigs are now being left behind to serve as artificial reefs where sea life can flourish after the drilling process is over. The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), the federal agency that regulates offshore oil and gas operations, reported that 43 retired platforms had been converted into artificial reefs between 2017 and 2020 through its Rigs-to-Reefs program . That brought the total number of converted structures in the Gulf past 500. These aren't temporary fixes. Once a jacket's drilling days are over, toppling its steel lattice structure in place, or partially submerging it, turns it into a permanent underwater habitat.The statistics presented by BSEE also reveal the reasons why states are always opting for this particular choice instead of the complete removal of the platforms. Over 100 species of fish have been identified around these platforms, and many of these are significant in commercial and recreational angling. These structures provide a surface for algae, sponges, individual coral colonies, and various other invertebrates to thrive on.The reasons behind their effectiveness are not only anecdotal. In a 2014 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , Jeremy Claisse of Occidental College and colleagues reported that California oil platforms had the highest secondary fish production per unit of seafloor area of any marine habitat studied to date, about an order of magnitude higher than other marine ecosystems, including estuaries, traditionally considered among the most productive on the planet. The researchers analyzed four Southern California platforms using hydroacoustics and trawls over 18 months, then converted the fish biomass they measured into standing stock and annual production per square meter of seafloor. Drawing on separate visual surveys of 16 platforms conducted over as long as 15 years by co-authors Milton Love and Ann Bull, the team estimated that platform fish communities produced roughly ten times more biomass than other marine habitats studied, with the platforms' midwater structure accounting for most of that production; the researchers attributed this largely to rockfish larvae settling and maturing on the platforms' hard vertical surfaces. The same paper found that, compared specifically to nearby natural rocky reefs at similar depths, the platforms produced more than 27 times as much fish biomass.This is significant in terms of the Gulf, because structures in the Gulf are more homogeneous despite being different from the environment in California. An eight-leg structure in the Gulf, for example, may support 12,000 to 14,000 fish at one time, according to the Coastal Marine Institute at Louisiana State University.This finding inevitably led to a natural inquiry: Is this true for the Gulf of Mexico, which has many more platforms than the California coast? According to the Bulletin of Marine Science, the study conducted by Kevin Boswell et al. investigated Freeport Sulphur Mine Artificial Reef, a platform turned into an artificial reef off the coast of Louisiana, which was the biggest reef structure in the northern Gulf of Mexico at the time. It was determined through the use of mobile acoustic sampling that there was five times less biomass and fish density at 10 metres and 16 times less at 30 metres from the reef structure. The Bulletin of Marine Science research also found that fish concentrated most heavily near the bottom of the water column rather than near the surface, a pattern that has practical implications for how platforms are toppled or partially removed during conversion.In combination, these two studies account for the biological principle behind BSEE's estimate of 43 platforms. As the research above suggests, the platforms' complex structure, not simple attraction, appears to be what drives the high fish production observed around them.None of this implies that choosing between removal and reefing is a straightforward task. By keeping the jacket in situ rather than hauling it to shore for disposal, companies reduce their costs, while coastal communities receive diving and fishing opportunities that would vanish following decommissioning of the platform. Yet, from the scientific basis of the project, California production calculations through to acoustic measurements in Louisiana, it becomes apparent that the environmental benefit is not coincidental. Given that fewer than 2,000 platforms are expected to remain for decommissioning in the Gulf over the next few years, the 43 projects registered by BSEE from 2017 to 2020 may represent only a small share of future reefing projects.
Article Summary: Federal agency says 43 platforms have been converted into artificial reefs. Over 100 species of fish have been identified around these platforms. These structures provide a surface for algae, sponges, individual coral colonies, and various other invertebrates to thrive on. California research measured record fish production on platform structures.

Article Title: In 2020, a Michigan medical student solved a poem and found a chest hidden somewhere in Wyoming for a decade; its 476 items later sold for over $1.3 million
Article Text:
AI Representation: A hidden treasure chest filled with gold and jewellery evokes the Wyoming treasure hunt solved through a cryptic poem. Image credits: Chatgpt

A Michigan medical student located the chest in 2020

Treasure Hunting as an American Subculture: The Thrill of the Chase

The search cost some searchers far more than money

The north aspect of Split Mountain rises above Mammoth Glacier in Wyoming's Wind River Range. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The auction sold 476 lots from the collection

A hunt that outlived its own mystery

For almost ten years, a bronze box filled with gold and jewelry was buried somewhere in the Rocky Mountains, drawing an estimated 350,000 hunters, according to Heritage Auctions, to roam through the mountains and canyons of America. Forrest Fenn, an art dealer in Santa Fe, hid the treasure in 2010 and published his memoir, The Thrill of the Chase, the same year, launching the hunt. The memoir contained a poem made up of 24 lines and nine clues. According to Fenn, the motivation behind the hiding of the chest was his diagnosis with kidney cancer in 1988, which appeared to be fatal initially but turned out to be nonfatal. The author finally hid the chest in 2010 and published his memoir during the same year so as to cheer people up after the Great Recession.According to Daniel Barbarisi's December 7, 2020, article in Outside magazine, "The Man Who Found Forrest Fenn's Treasure," the search ended in June 2020 when Jonathan "Jack" Stuef, a 32-year-old medical student from Michigan, found the chest after decoding the clues in Forrest Fenn's poem. The man discovered the poem in 2018 on Twitter and got obsessed with it to such an extent that he admitted that he was thinking about the poem for hours every day.CBS News Colorado (2022) states that Jack Stuef communicated with Forrest Fenn after locating the chest in June 2020. In the months preceding his death in September 2020, Forrest Fenn publicly disclosed that the treasure was found. Stuef's identity remained confidential for six months. According to court filings, he came forward in December 2020 after a U.S. District Court ruling required Fenn's estate to disclose his name and address as part of a lawsuit filed by attorney Barbara Andersen.The poem was kept in Fenn's self-published memoir for ten years before anyone could break it, and the sheer volume of the reaction it received became the focus of academic research later on. Psychologist Alan King of the University of North Dakota built a survey of people connected to the hunt and published his findings in, in the journal Human Arenas . Based on survey responses from a sample of chase participants, King's study estimated that approximately two million American adults had some association with the hunt, of whom an estimated 433,013 were experienced, competitive searchers. Furthermore, the study revealed that 80% of a well-experienced sample of 249 chasers regarded Fenn and the treasure hunt highly, whereas approximately 10% thought that the chase may turn out to be an addiction for them.Indeed, there were many risks involved. CBS News reported that at least four people died while searching for Forrest Fenn's treasure chest. CBS News also reported that a man was arrested after digging up graves in Yellowstone National Park while trying to find the treasure chest. Local officials in Wyoming and Montana always commented on the difficulties associated with rescue operations when searchers took marked paths but kept it a secret from everyone, including their families. As reported by ABC News (July 2017), the New Mexico State Police Chief, Pete Kassetas, officially requested that Forrest Fenn end his treasure search due to a death incident involving a Colorado pastor looking for the treasure. Fenn ignored the request, as he said that the treasure was indeed real.This subculture has created a community of devoted bloggers who would analyze every word of Fenn's poem in order to determine its true meaning. In one of his papers, The Pursuit of Unattainable Goals , published in Possibility Studies & Society, King returned to the same case to build out what he called liminal commitment theory, a framework for understanding why people commit years of their lives to goals that are, by most objective measures, extremely unlikely to be reached. As per the authors, liminality refers to the process of change of identity, which occurs over time through rites of passage. King's theory of liminal commitment builds on the Fenn case as an example, arguing that just as there are alluring aspects to being a treasure hunter, similar motivations may drive people to pursue other unattainable ventures. Unattainability refers to the distance of the goal from the subject and low levels of perceived attainability.In an article released by Heritage Auctions titled “Heritage Auctions Opens Forrest Fenn’s Treasure Chest to Collectors”, dated September 19, 2022, the recovered treasure chest and all the objects contained therein were sold to Tesouro Sagrado Holdings, LLC, a private buyer. According to Heritage Auctions, Jack Stuef did not disclose the sale price. During December of that year, the new owner enlisted the services of Heritage Auctions in Dallas for the sale of 476 items in an online auction spanning one month. The owner retained a portion of the chest's original contents, which were excluded from the sale; the remaining 476 lots went to auction. At the close of bidding, all 476 lots sold, with 1,643 bidders participating and a total of $1,307,946 generated.The item that sold at the highest price was an Alaskan gold nugget weighing 549 grams, roughly the weight of nine to eleven large eggs and fetching a sum of $55,200. The second highest-priced item in the collection was a little wax-sealed glass jar alleged to contain a 20,000-word autobiography written in micro-text and placed in the chest by Fenn. As he revealed in his autobiography, Fenn included the story to ensure that whoever discovered the treasure would also learn something about him, the man who had hidden it.The precise location of the chest was never officially revealed by Fenn, and even Stuef has kept it to himself, only mentioning that it was somewhere in Wyoming. However, some participants of the treasure hunt have speculated that the chest may have been located somewhere in Yellowstone National Park. What Heritage Auctions and King's research confirm is the scale of the phenomenon: a self-published poem drew hundreds of thousands of people into the hunt, and the treasure was eventually found years later.
Article Summary: For almost ten years, a bronze box filled with gold and jewelry was buried somewhere in the Rocky Mountains. Forrest Fenn, an art dealer in Santa Fe, hid the treasure in 2010 and published his memoir, The Thrill of the Chase, the same year, launching the hunt. The poem was kept in Fenn's self-published memoir for ten years before anyone could break it. A Michigan medical student located the chest in 2020.

Article Title: Meet Kent Hups, the Colorado teacher who spotted three strange toes in North Dakota and helped uncover the first adult T. rex trackway
Article Text:
Representative Image of North Dakota's badlands showcasing dinosaur footprints and the discovery of T. rex tracks (AI Generated Image)

Lyson wanted a pattern, not just one footprint

The Hell Creek Formation rarely preserves dinosaur footprints

Nearby T. rex fossils helped identify the trackmaker

The tracks could reveal how T. rex moved

Kent Hups, a Colorado high school teacher and amateur fossil hunter, was looking for an easier route out of a narrow, rocky valley in North Dakota's badlands in 2025 when he noticed something unusual protruding from the ground. To Hups, who had spent about 30 years searching for ancient footprints as a hobby, the lumpy, wedge-shaped rock looked like three giant toes. He was volunteering with a fossil-digging team led by palaeontologist Tyler Lyson when he contacted him about the discovery. Lyson was sceptical and wanted more than a single unusual shape before accepting it as a dinosaur track. Further excavation revealed a sequence of four three-toed footprints stretching about 23 feet across the hillside. Researchers have identified an adult Tyrannosaurus rex as the most likely trackmaker, making it the first described trackway likely left by an adult T. rex. The approximately 66.5-million-year-old trail provides evidence of the dinosaur in motion, something that fossilised bones cannot show on their own.Hups found the first footprint while prospecting for fossils in the Hell Creek Formation.
